description.value: The study examined how emotional valence modulates effective connectivity within a right-hemisphere prefrontal-amygdala-fusiform face area network during dynamic facial affect processing.

spans.text: Our findings indicate changes in coupling strength as a function of emotional valence within the prefrontal-AMY network.

design.value: Thirty-three healthy volunteers completed a 6-min fMRI dynamic face-matching and shape-matching task involving positive, negative, and neutral facial-valence blocks and shape-matching blocks, followed by whole-brain GLM analyses and dynamic causal modeling.

spans.text: All participants completed a 6-min fMRI dynamic face-matching and shape-matching task ( Fig. 1 A ), which is based on the static task used by Hariri et al. (2002) .
We used face images from the Radboud face database ( Langner et al., 2010 ), including the faces of 38 white actors (19 females).

task_description.value: Participants matched a dynamic target image with one of two static probe images by facial expression or shape.

spans.text: In each trial, participants were presented with a dynamic target item and two static probe images below it, one of which matched with the target item with regard to shape or facial expression.
Face-matching and shape-matching blocks had a length of 20 s and were presented alternatingly.

instructions.value: Subjects were instructed to match either the left or the right static item at the bottom with the dynamic item on top and to press either the left or the right button with their dominant hand on a response-pad to indicate their choice as soon as they recognized which probe matched.

stimuli.value: Emotional faces and polygons; positive blocks included happy, surprised, and neutral faces, negative blocks included sad and disgusted faces, and neutral blocks included neutral and surprised faces.

spans.text: In total, we presented six face-matching blocks (30 trials, 10 trials per valence), two positively valenced, including happy, surprised and neutral faces, two negatively valenced, sad and disgusted faces, and two neutrally valenced, neutral and surprised faces

DCM is a hypothesis-driven Bayesian model comparison procedure for inferring effective connectivity between brain regions.

model_settings.value: Four-region model comprising the LPFC, MPFC, AMY, and FFA; 256 models grouped into four families; valence modulation varied across connections; Bayesian model selection and Bayesian model averaging were performed.

spans.text: Modulation by valence was varied systematically across connections between MPFC and LPFC, and MPFC and AMY in all possible modulation patterns, spanning a model space of 256 models.

level.value: subject-level DCM with random-effects family-wise Bayesian model selection across subjects

spans.text: We performed random-effects family-wise Bayesian model selection (BMS; Penny et al., 2010 ) as implemented in SPM12 to compute the expected posterior probabilities and the exceedance probabilities of model families within our sample.

spans.text: We used Bayesian model averaging (BMA) across models to make further inferences on the significance of connections and modulation by valence ( Penny et al., 2010 ).
